---
title: "Catalog and Runtime Identity"
subtitle: "How is source provenance portable across wheels, Git, modules, and Notebooks?"
toc-depth: 2
---

**Status:** `CONVERGING` implementation design.

## Prove a factory when it creates a component

Constructing an empty custom `Library` remains ordinary, inspectable Python.
Exact source proof becomes mandatory only when one of its factories would
return a `ComponentInstance`. The resulting Plan records the catalog module,
qualified class, factory name, provenance kind, and source digest; neither a
display name nor a memory address is sufficient.

For a custom catalog, canonical `catalog_id` is `module:qualified_class`.
Multiple immutable instances of the same class therefore share catalog
semantics; component identity still includes the invoked factory and its bound
arguments. The built-in singleton is the deliberate exception: its reserved
identity is `scnsim.components`, with public symbol `components`. The private
concrete Python class is implementation detail and may be renamed without
renaming every primitive Plan.

SCNSim resolves the first applicable portable provenance form in this order:

| Source | Canonical evidence |
|---|---|
| installed wheel | normalized distribution name/version and sorted `RECORD` rows with their content hashes |
| editable Git package | Git object ID, package-relative source file list and bytes, plus a digest of the dirty package-tree overlay |
| imported source module | logical module name and the complete normalized bytes of its defining `.py` module |
| Notebook definition | dedented UTF-8/NFC class and factory source with normalized newlines |

For a wheel, SCNSim parses `RECORD` as CSV, normalizes separators, preserves
the declared hash/size fields (including the ordinary empty self row), sorts by
distribution-relative path, verifies every declared file hash, and hashes the
canonical row list. Distribution names use normalized package-name spelling;
versions use installed metadata spelling.

For editable Git, `source_sha256` hashes a sorted manifest of package-relative
path, Git file mode, and current file bytes beneath the catalog's Python package
root. The dirty-overlay digest covers modified, deleted, and untracked
non-ignored files relative to the recorded commit; cache/build/VCS metadata is
excluded. Clean trees use the SHA-256 of the empty canonical overlay. Notebook
source hashes the class and invoked factory definitions in definition order.

An ordinary imported source module uses `module_source` only when no installed
wheel or editable-install identity owns it. SCNSim obtains the defining regular
`.py` file, decodes its declared Python source encoding, normalizes newlines and
NFC, encodes UTF-8, and hashes the complete module text. The logical import name
remains part of `catalog_id`; the source path, file timestamps, inode, and Git
checkout location do not. Bytecode-only modules, extension modules, ambiguous
origins, and unreadable source fail before component creation.

V1 does not recursively hash an arbitrary Python import graph for
`module_source`. Project-local code that affects a factory must remain in that
defining module or move into an installed/editable package with closed source
provenance. Built-in SCNSim factories called by the module retain their own
catalog identity, and the resulting complete component graph remains part of
Plan identity.

Absolute checkout/venv paths, Notebook execution count, cell or temporary
filename, line number, kernel ID, and object address are excluded. A Notebook
factory whose source is no longer available through Python's source/line cache
fails before creating the component; SCNSim does not ask the author to invent a
manual catalog ID.

Built-in `scnsim.components` still binds the installed-wheel or editable-Git
source identity of SCNSim. A custom package calling a built-in primitive
therefore records both the custom factory provenance and the exact built-in
catalog provenance; only the private class name is excluded.

## Separate semantic runtime from the machine

The request binds a semantic runtime containing:

- SCNSim Python and Julia source digests;
- the operation-level numerical algorithm ID;
- exact Julia version; and
- committed `Project.toml` and `Manifest.toml` hashes.

The Python source digest uses a sorted manifest of package-relative path, file
mode, and bytes for shipped `.py` files plus every runtime-consumed schema and
static metadata file, including the identity schema bundle. The Julia digest
does the same for the shipped `.jl` tree. Generated caches, checkout paths, and
VCS metadata are excluded. Changing any manifest entry creates a different
semantic runtime.

An operation-level algorithm ID is transitive, not a label for only the outer
driver. In particular,
`scnsim.direct_cmaes.cmaes_jl_0_2_6_state_replay.v2` binds the exact CMA,
unit-box transform, Direct operator, selected quantity, continuation, and
replay-certificate algorithms it invokes. Changing any dependency requires a
new outer ID even when the `OptimizationSpec` bytes are unchanged. The request
continues to carry one operation ID rather than an unordered set whose
composition would be ambiguous.

The exact Julia version and algorithm ID come from package-owned static runtime
metadata, not from host discovery. This lets Python recompute request identity
during `resolve()` without starting Julia. JuliaPkg may reuse a system Julia
only when its complete version equals that declared patch; the chosen
executable's bytes remain attempt evidence.

The attempt separately records the actual Julia executable hash, OS,
architecture, CPU description, Julia thread count, BLAS thread count, and BLAS
vendor. Available host core count and those execution resources do not rename
the request. Every V1 numerical slice launches Julia and BLAS single-threaded
to reduce avoidable drift; the observed values are still verified and stored.

`resolve()` never prepares Julia or compares current hardware. It verifies the
stored request, receipt, Result, and artifacts. A later execution under a
different semantic runtime is a different request, while the same semantic
runtime on another machine may reuse the verified request already present in a
relocated workspace.
